title: Can, may, don't need to
goal: Express ability with *-a olmoq*, ask permission with *mumkin*, and tell "not allowed" apart from "not necessary" — two things that often get mixed up.

telling *mumkin emas* (not allowed) apart from *kerak emas* (not necessary)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kirsam boʻladimi?
dialogs.intro: Budi knocks on the door of a lecturer's office. He needs a signature on a scholarship form.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Assalamu alaikum, professor. May I come in?

lines.speaker: Ustoz:
lines.id: Wa alaikum assalam. Come in, please do.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bir savolim bor edi. Vaqtingiz bormi?
lines.id: I have a question. Do you have a moment?
lines.literal: one question-my exists was. time-your exists-?

lines.speaker: Ustoz:
lines.text: Bor, ammo koʻp emas. Oʻn daqiqadan keyin majlisim bor.
lines.id: Yes, but not much. I have a meeting in ten minutes.
lines.literal: exists, but much not. ten minute-from after meeting-my exists.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tez boʻladi. Bu hujjatga imzo qoʻya olasizmi?
lines.id: It'll be quick. Could you sign this document?
lines.literal: quick becomes. this document-to signature put can-you-?

lines.speaker: Ustoz:
lines.id: Let me see... Do you need it today?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Not today — I'm handing it in tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Ustoz:
lines.text: Yaxshi. Lekin bu yerga qalam bilan yozish mumkin emas.
lines.id: Good. But you can't write in pencil here.

lines.id: May I borrow your pen for a minute?

lines.speaker: Ustoz:
lines.id: Here you go. There — I've signed it too.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Katta rahmat, ustoz! Endi ketsam boʻladimi?
lines.id: Thank you so much, professor! May I go now?

notes: **Kirsam boʻladimi? is the most polite way to ask permission.** The pattern: stem + *-sa* + possessive ending + *boʻladimi*. Literally "if I come in, is it OK?". The *-sa* form is fully unpacked in unit 19; for now just learn the pattern.

**Kerak emas ≠ mumkin emas.** *Bugun kerak emas* means "not needed today" — you may, but you don't have to. *Yozish mumkin emas* means "you may not write" — it's forbidden. Swap them and you could break a rule while feeling perfectly polite.
**Imzo qoʻymoq = to sign**, literally "to put a signature". Another compound verb, and as usual *qoʻymoq* loses its original meaning here.
**Majlis means meeting** — an Arabic word for an assembly or council. In Uzbekistan it's also the name of the parliament: *Oliy Majlis*.

grammars.title: -a olmoq: being able to do something
body: The formula: stem + *-a* (or *-y* after a vowel) + a conjugated *olmoq*. Two separate words, but said as one.

rows: I managed / didn't manage to go

after: ⚠️ **The negative goes on *olmoq*, not on the stem.** *Bora olmayman* — not *bormay olaman*. This mistake is instantly noticeable, so practice the negative as much as the positive.

Don't confuse this with *bilmoq* + *-(i)sh* in unit 16. *Suzishni bilaman* = "I can swim" (I've learned; it's a skill I have). *Suza olaman* = "I can swim" (right now, in this situation, I'm able to).
The past *-a olmadim* is very handy for apologizing: *Kela olmadim, kechirasiz* = "I couldn't come, sorry".

grammars.title: Mumkin, kerak emas, mumkin emas
body: Three expressions that cover all of permission and prohibition at A1.
after: Note that they all use the *-(i)sh* form from unit 16: *kirish*, *chekish*, *borish*, *toʻlash*. The verb has to become a noun before *mumkin* or *kerak* can follow it.
For a more casual permission, *boʻladimi?* — "OK?" — is enough. To refuse politely: *Kechirasiz, boʻlmaydi* (sorry, that's not possible).
Signs in Uzbekistan often use short forms: *Chekish taqiqlanadi* (smoking prohibited), *Kirish taqiqlangan* (no entry), *Ehtiyot boʻling!* (caution).

blocks.text: Not romantic vocabulary, but unavoidable for anyone living, studying, or working in Uzbekistan.

⚠️ Almost every word in this table comes from Arabic: *hujjat* (proof → document), *ariza* (petition → application), *ruxsat* (license → permission), *idora* (administration → office), *muhr* (seal), *nusxa* (manuscript → copy). If you know any Arabic, Persian, or Turkish, it pays off again here.
Useful sentences: *Bu hujjatga imzo kerakmi?* (does this document need a signature?), *Nusxasini olsam boʻladimi?* (may I take a copy?), *Ruxsat bering, iltimos* (may I, please).
Ten signs found on doors, walls, and windows all over Uzbekistan.
*Bepul* literally means "without money" — the Persian prefix *be-* means "without", a cousin of *-siz*. You'll meet it again in *bechora* (poor thing, "without a way out") and *behuda* (in vain).

Note too that many signs are still written in Cyrillic, especially on older buildings and in small towns: **ОЧИҚ** = *ochiq*, **ЁПИҚ** = *yopiq*. If you meet a sign you can't read, it's most likely not another language — just another alphabet.
